human_tolerance.notes: Breeds in open shrubby country including towns, and 'sometimes using artificial sites such as telephone poles near towns' for its nest; the winter range is a separate area entirely, so a street-block garden is a breeding-season home rather than year-round cover.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Judgement window. The article gives the breeding habitat ('open shrubby country with scattered trees in the south-central states of Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, western portions of Louisiana, Arkansas, and Missouri') and 'Clutches contain three to six eggs' with both parents feeding the young, but no calendar months; the window is placed over the spring and summer of that breeding range.

phases.name: absent
phases.note: 'They migrate through Texas and eastern Mexico to their winter non-breeding range, from southern Mexico to Panama.' The absent phase covers the wintering range and most of the passage; the day boundaries are the author's judgement, with pre-migratory roosts and southbound flocks in late summer as the article describes.

taxonomy.note: Gmelin 1789, Tyrannus forficatus - 'formally described in 1789 by the German naturalist Johann Friedrich Gmelin'; family Tyrannidae per the GBIF backbone and ITIS TSN 178293. The article also notes 'The species is monotypic: no subspecies are recognised.'

common_names.note: en/fr/es labels; the English name follows the Wikipedia article title, and the fr/es labels the Wikidata sitelink titles. The article also gives 'swallow-tailed flycatcher' and 'scissorstail' as alternative English names.

range.note: Breeding range from the distribution section: 'open shrubby country with scattered trees in the south-central states of Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, western portions of Louisiana, Arkansas, and Missouri west to far eastern New Mexico and northeastern Mexico'; winter range 'from southern Mexico to Panama'; vagrants 'as far north as southern Canada and Upstate New York, as far east as Florida and Georgia, and in the West Indies' are excluded from the native list. Koppen classes are the author's judgement of the described range.

traits.limb_count.note: Biped: two legs, the forelimbs modified as wings.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: A perching insectivore that 'may catch them in flight (hawking)' after 'waiting on a perch', plus the 'spectacular aerial display during courtship with his long tail forks streaming out behind him', so a hop and flight are the two gaits.

traits.thermoregulation.note: Endotherm: a bird that arrives on its breeding grounds in spring and leaves in autumn.

traits.skin.note: Feathers: plumage described in detail in the Description section.

traits.flight.note: Powered flight: aerial hawking, a courtship display in the air, and a migration between breeding and wintering ranges.

traits.metamorphosis.note: None: 'Immature birds are duller in color and have shorter tails', a feathered young bird rather than a metamorphic larva.

traits.nest_type.note: 'They build a cup nest in isolated trees or shrubs, sometimes using artificial sites such as telephone poles near towns.'

traits.perching.note: Perches to hunt: it forages by 'waiting on a perch and then flying out to catch them in flight'.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: the validator bands a bird under 0.05 kg as Tiny, and 0.035 kg falls in that band.

traits.mass_kg.note: The article gives only a maximum, 'the weight is up to 43 g (1.5 oz)'. mass_kg is authored at 0.035 kg, roughly four fifths of that ceiling, because the article also describes smaller individuals in the population ('Immature birds are duller in color and have shorter tails'). It is a stated estimate, not a sourced mean.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: The upper bound is the article's 'the weight is up to 43 g (1.5 oz)'. The lower bound is authored, since the article gives no minimum; 0.025 kg reflects the smaller females the article describes ('the female's tail is up to 30% shorter').

traits.length_m.note: The article gives maxima only: 'At maturity, the male may be up to 15 in (38 cm) in length, while the female's tail is up to 30% shorter', and 'A lot of these birds have been reported to be more than 40 cm (16 in)'. 0.38 is the stated male maximum, used because the article gives no range; it understates the many birds reported over 40 cm.

traits.lifespan_y.note: The article gives no lifespan figure for this species. Authored at 6 years, a rough figure for a medium-sized flycatcher, as a stated estimate rather than a sourced number.

traits.diet.note: 'In the summer, scissor-tailed flycatchers feed mainly on insects (grasshoppers, robber-flies, and dragonflies) ... For additional food in the winter they will also eat some berries.' The 0.9 insect and 0.1 berry shares follow the words 'mainly' and 'some', and the berries carry a months restriction to the winter.

traits.social.note: The article does not describe pair bonds or group size, only 'Both parents feed the young' and that 'Pre-migratory roosts and flocks flying south may contain as many as 1000 birds'. Pair is used for the breeding unit, with a small range that covers a pair and any young; the thousand-bird figure is a migratory flock, not a foraging group, so it is not used here.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Diurnal: it waits on a perch in daylight, hawks insects in flight, and the whole behavioural account is daytime activity.

traits.defense.note: Mob: 'Like other kingbirds, they are very aggressive in defending their nest.'

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: it hunts from exposed perches including 'artificial sites such as telephone poles near towns' and flushes easily, but its nest defence is aggressive rather than wary.

habitat.use.note: 'Their breeding habitat is open shrubby country with scattered trees', it waits on a perch and flies out to catch insects in the air, and it nests in trees, shrubs and on poles. The split between the aerial hawking, the arboreal perches and the ground is the author's judgement from that description, with the aerial share the largest because hawking is how the summer diet is caught.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Roosts and sings from an exposed perch - a tree, a shrub or a telephone pole - rather than nesting in a cavity.

habitat.resources.note: The invertebrate weight follows the diet, with berry carrying the winter months the article gives; nest_cup is the cup nest and perch the hunting and singing perch, which is the resource this bird is most tied to.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: urban_affinity and uses_gardens from nesting 'in isolated trees or shrubs, sometimes using artificial sites such as telephone poles near towns' and from the breeding habitat including the settled parts of the south-central states; Adapter rather than Exploiter because the whole population leaves for Mexico and Panama outside the breeding season, so no part of the year is a year-round urban resident. light_max, flight_distance_m and road_mortality are judgement values, the article giving no figures.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'They migrate through Texas and eastern Mexico to their winter non-breeding range, from southern Mexico to Panama', with pre-migratory roosts and southbound flocks, so the record is a full migration with an absent phase covering the wintering range.

seasonal.phases.note: The article states the breeding range, the wintering range and 'Clutches contain three to six eggs', but gives no calendar months for either. Both phase boundaries are the author's judgement, placed so that the breeding phase covers the spring and summer of the south-central US breeding range and the absent phase covers the wintering range and most of the passage.

seasonal.life_stages.note: The article gives the clutch size ('Clutches contain three to six eggs') and that 'Both parents feed the young', but no incubation or nestling period. duration_days and scale are a rough judgement of the nestling period for a bird of this size, not a sourced figure.

look.note: Plumage from the Description section: 'Adult birds have pale gray heads and upper parts, light underparts, salmon-pink flanks and undertail coverts, and dark gray wings. Axillars and patch on underwing coverts are red. Their extremely long, forked tails, which are black on top and white on the underside, are characteristic and unmistakable.' Proportions are judgement, with a very long tail as the article's 'extremely long, forked tails' requires; the flank parts carry the salmon-pink and the long_tail part the deep forked tail.

behavior.note: This species ships its own behavior.json (bt-perch-sally-flycatcher-v1) rather than using a shared program, for two reasons. First, the article documents no vocalization at all, while every shared songbird program sings from a song perch and calls an alarm, so using one would leave the record pointing at calls it cannot source. Second, the bird's actual foraging is perch-and-sally - 'waiting on a perch and then flying out to catch them in flight (hawking)' - rather than the hop-and-peck ground foraging the shared program does. The program is otherwise the shared perching-songbird pattern with the song and alarm branches removed, so it duplicates as little as possible. All params are authored: a long flee distance for a bird that flushes from a high perch, insect-led forage, and a spring-summer nest window.
